KiwiFibre Innovations

Fibre Extraction Machine

Turning plant fibres, where every fibre is unique, into a composite material with consistent material properties requires a lot of iteration. It requires identifying which natural variables in an uncountably long list have the most significant impact on fibre properties. It also requires a machine where processing variables can be accurately known and tightly controlled. By iterating through the combinations of natural and machine variables, the recipe for obtaining optimal natural fibres can be found. This is the motivation behind KiwiFibre's Fibre Extraction Machine development.

Harakeke fibre mills used to cover the full length and breadth of New Zealand. However, the peak of the industry was over a century ago, and every mill has been shut down or abandoned for several decades. Developing this machine therefore required examining literal museum pieces and 100-year-old documents to understand the underlying mechanisms involved in the fibre extraction process. This gave us a starting point for our initial prototype. The design of this prototype was improved through testing and iterative development, which informed the design of a 2nd generation machine.

This machine integrated novel features proven on the first prototype into its core design, was delivered to the client, and has been used to demonstrate that high-quality harakeke fibre can be produced at scale. This was achieved by our small, interdisciplinary team with the tight timelines and budget constraints of an early startup.

I've been heavily involved in this project from my first day at KiwiFibre. As the sole qualified engineer I have worked on every aspect from research and conceptual design through to final assembly, testing and operations. Recently I was involved in a pilot production run, using this machine to produce harakeke fibre at scale out on a farm for 3 months. This not only demonstrates the feasibility of harakeke fibre production, but also the robust design and construction of our fibre extraction machine.

  • Research, conceptual design ideation and evaluation of new mechanical systems.
  • Analysis and detailed design of bespoke mechanical systems (rotating elements and power transmission, etc.).
  • Implementing Health and Safety features to meet relevant standards (ISO 14120).
  • CAD and technical drawings (Fusion 360) of bespoke components. Applying DFMA principles and communicating with contracted fabricators.
  • Final assembly and delivery, followed by testing and iterative development of machine design and processes to optimise fibre production.

Novel Fibre Extraction Methods: Prototypes

The overarching strategy for our current fibre extraction machine was to take an existing and proven concept and iteratively improve it until we could produce fibre that met our specifications. A straightforward, low-risk approach.

But what if there was a way to leapfrog previously understood methods with a completely new fibre extraction method? A completely new proposed technique utilising high-pressure water may be able to produce fibre at the quality KiwiFibre requires. This project aimed to deliver test rigs to investigate this potential pathway.

This idea was proposed by one of our clients and the project was pursued collaboratively with them. I personally sat in on the first few meetings discussing the project, watching as business details were hashed out and ideas began to crystallise. Eventually my role was to translate all the nebulous ideas, approaches and desires into an engineering project proposal with clearly defined scope and deliverables. The final proposal included delivery of 2 distinct test rigs, which used in tandem could be used to test the widest range of relevant variables. Results of testing with these machines, if successful, would inform the design of a potential future pilot production-scale system. This allowed the viability of this new method to be investigated while minimising up-front risk and cost.

Everyone was satisfied and the project went ahead as proposed. After going through the motions of the design and build process, the test rigs were delivered on time and on budget. This provided me with holistic project experience from proposal to delivery, and I got to take ownership over much of the design process.

  • Turning nebulous ideas and stakeholder input into a collaborative project proposal that satisfied our internal requirements and our client's.
  • Conceptual design ideation and evaluation of 2 test rigs, including a brief report for our client on the designs chosen and the justification behind them.
  • Analysis and detailed design of 2 test rigs including pneumatic systems, high-pressure water and rotating machinery.
  • Assembly, commissioning and operation of the 2 test rigs.

Fibre Washing Systems

Testing of our initial prototype fibre extraction system produced a significant amount of fibre that we could send to manufacturing partners for them to assess. They promptly told us that there was far too much dust and waste material in the fibre to be run through their processing lines at scale. This prompted the development of a fibre washing system.

Historical flax mills used huge amounts of water, generally drawing directly from, and dumping waste into the nearest waterway. This is obviously not a suitable approach in a modern context, so our system had to use water more efficiently. This system was also being developed in parallel to our fibre extraction machine, which took up most of our time and resource. As such, the washing system had to be delivered rapidly and on a very minimal budget.

Given the potentially complex and unpredictable behaviour of the fibre during washing, it was decided that the best approach was rapid, iterative development of low-cost washing prototypes. Each iteration would optimise the configuration of the system and increase the total water flow rate until a suitable system was delivered.

The latest iteration of the washing system went from design to delivery in a few months and came in under our very thin budget. It circulates ~400 L/min of water and uses an arrangement of nozzles to splay out the fibre bundles, minimising the amount of tangling and matting. This system was recently put through its paces during our most recent fibre production run, and worked flawlessly for several months of flat-out running in a harsh agricultural setting.

Some of my key contributions to this project include:

  • Developed functional prototype suitable for pilot scale production from concept to delivery in under 3 months.
  • Fluid systems design, balancing head loss vs component cost and optimising nozzle geometry to maximise washing characteristics.
  • CAD and CAM to produce bespoke components using limited in-house manufacturing capability.
  • Assembly and delivery of functional system to pilot production site. Testing regime to verify system met design requirements and optimise settings for production.

Fibre Tensile Testing Method

Most recently, I have been developing an in-house methodology for fibre tensile testing. The goal is to develop a quick and economical process for determining the tensile strength of natural fibres for quality control and iterative improvement of fibre production methods. This involved using a process laid out in a published research paper used to determine the strength of fibres from tensile testing of composite fibre bundles. I modified the samples to be in line with ISO standards for composite 3-point bending tests.

I have also developed sample production best practices and methods for analysing sample cross-sections under a microscope to accurately determine the sample's fibre volume fraction.

  • Adapting a published research methodology into an ISO-aligned in-house test process
  • Developing sample production best practices from scratch
  • Building a microscopy-based method for determining fibre volume fraction from cross-sections
  • Delivering a fast, low-cost alternative to standard testing, suited to a resource-constrained startup
UC Final Year Project

Kea Aerospace

Lithium-ion batteries tend to expand and contract over many charge/discharge cycles, causing them to degrade over time. To counter this, batteries are sometimes kept under constant compression. This minimises the swelling, decreasing the drop in performance over time. This is key for optimising the performance of Kea Aerospace's High Altitude Long Endurance vehicle, as energy storage and management are vital.

In order to get the maximum increase in performance, the correct pressure needs to be applied to the batteries over time. This therefore requires a test rig to determine this optimal pressure behaviour for a given type of battery cell. This project was challenging due to a significant change in scope partway through the year. We also faced a very limited budget, meaning we had to find creative ways of leveraging what resources we did have available through the uni to deliver a system that met the client's requirements.

  • Found ways to minimise cost to complete the project with a minimal budget under tight timelines, while meeting strict design requirements in an aerospace setting.
  • Primarily responsible for designing and procuring pneumatic components to satisfy design requirements and fit within our budget. Also responsible for obtaining a suitable load cell.
  • Exposure to sensors and data acquisition.
University of Canterbury

UC Aerospace / UC Flightclub / Glider Design

During my time at uni I pursued several aerospace-related projects, both as a part of my studies and extracurricularly. During 3rd year, some of my friends and I completed UC Aerospace's Level 1 rocketry program. This involves learning the fundamentals of amateur high-power rocketry, then assembling and launching a 1.4m tall rocket. Our rocket included a basic barometer in the nose, which we used to determine the apogee at roughly 900m.

This led me and 2 other ex-fixed-wing teammates to found UC Flightclub, which focused on fixed-wing RC planes. Our immediate focus was simply getting the club up and running, but we hoped the club would pursue a similar large fixed-wing design project. At the same time I was completing a self-selected design report on the aerodynamic design of a large, 2m wingspan RC glider for one of my 4th-year aerospace papers. This report included using XFOIL and XFLR5 software to simulate characteristics such as L/D, and stability calculations to determine tail size, wing position, etc. This project is something I still think about, and would like to tackle again on my own someday.

  • Completed UC Aerospace's Level 1 rocketry program, from build through to launch and apogee tracking.
  • Co-founded UC Flightclub, a fixed-wing RC plane club.
  • Wrote a full aerodynamic design report for a 2m wingspan RC glider, using XFOIL and XFLR5.
